scheme: ALA-LC romanization of Urdu (without dots under the Arabic letters; ṭ, ḍ, ṛ for the retroflex consonants, ṉ for the nasal)
en: Better than all the world is our Hindustan;
we are its nightingales, it is our garden.
If we are in a foreign land, the heart stays in the homeland:
count us, too, to be there, where our heart is.
That mountain, highest of all, neighbour of the sky,
it is our sentry, it is our guardian.
In its lap play thousands of rivers,
by whose life our garden is the envy of paradise.
O water of the river Ganga! Do you remember those days
when our caravan came down to your bank?
Religion does not teach us to keep enmity among ourselves;
we are of Hind, our homeland is Hindustan.
Greece and Egypt and Rome have all vanished from the world,
but to this day our name and trace remain.
There is something in it, that our being is not wiped out,
though for centuries the turning of time has been our enemy.
Iqbal! We have no confidant in the world:
what does anyone know of our hidden pain!
rom: sāre jahāṉ se achchhā Hindūstāṉ hamārā
ham bulbuleṉ haiṉ is kī, yih gulistāṉ hamārā
ghurbat meṉ hoṉ agar ham, rahtā hai dil vatan meṉ
samjho vahīṉ hameṉ bhī dil ho jahāṉ hamārā
parbat vuh sab se ūṉchā, hamsāyah āsmāṉ kā
vuh santarī hamārā, vuh pāsbāṉ hamārā
godī meṉ kheltī haiṉ us kī hazāroṉ nadiyāṉ
gulshan hai jin ke dam se rashk-i jināṉ hamārā
ai āb-i rūd-i Gangā! vuh din haiṉ yād tujh ko?
utrā tire kināre jab kārvāṉ hamārā
mazhab nahīṉ sikhātā āpas meṉ bair rakhnā
Hindī haiṉ ham, vatan hai Hindūstāṉ hamārā
Yūnān o Misr o Rūmā sab miṭ gaʾe jahāṉ se
ab tak magar hai bāqī nām o nishāṉ hamārā
kuchh bāt hai kih hastī miṭtī nahīṉ hamārī
sadiyoṉ rahā hai dushman daur-i zamāṉ hamārā
Iqbāl! koʾī mahram apnā nahīṉ jahāṉ meṉ
maʿlūm kyā kisī ko dard-i nihāṉ hamārā!
notes: line 2.1: 'ghurbat', being away from home, exile (also poverty).
line 3.1: the mountain is the Himalaya, unnamed in the poem.
line 4.2: 'jinān', the gardens of paradise; 'dam', breath or life: the rivers give the garden its life.
line 5.2: the caravan coming down to the Ganges is the arrival of the poet's forebears (or of a people) in India; the sense is not spelled out.
line 6.2: 'Hindī' here means a person of Hind, India, not the language.
line 8.1: literally 'there is some matter (reason) that our existence does not perish'.
line 9.1: Iqbal names himself, as Urdu poets do in the last couplet; 'mahram', one who shares one's secrets.
